blocks.md: This lesson follows **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** in *Closed-Loop Evaluation* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Closed-Loop Evaluation, § Historical Perspective and Further Reading
blocks.md: The statistical foundations of closed-loop evaluation were established long before autonomous systems encountered physical hardware. Standard textbook treatments of binomial confidence intervals rely on asymptotic normality, yet normal approximations fail near the extreme boundaries (TrialSuccessProbability approx 0 or TrialSuccessProbability approx 1) where robot qualification and safety certification operate. @wilson1927probable resolved the degeneracy of the textbook interval at zero failures by inverting the score test, ensuring that confidence intervals would not collapse to zero width on a spotless empirical record.

questions.q: The section **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Early acceptance is valid only under a boundary declared in advance (Wald's SPRT), and comparing two checkpoints needs interleaved, randomized, blinded runs on one unit.

At zero failures the Wald interval collapses, so a clean record is inverted exactly (failure bound about 3/n), which makes twenty clean runs consistent with a one-in-seven failure rate and makes every added nine cost about ten times the trials.

The evaluation record binds a bounded claim to its target ODD, configuration digests, sampling protocol, complete outcome log, exact statistics, and the catalog of unsupported gaps, which become runtime obligations.
Task completion, proposer autonomy, and supervisory burden are separate channels, and an intervened run is an autonomy failure, never a success that was cut short (the censored trial fallacy).
